Pitch Notation from Do: Letter Names, Clefs and Accidentals

Chapter 1 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom for students who already read and write with movable do: letter names, clefs, octave registers, accidentals and enharmonic notes as names for the staff they already read.

This page goes with Chapter 1, Basic Concepts of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.

You already know this. You read and write tonal patterns on the staff: you find do from the do signature and read the rest from there. This chapter gives every line and space a fixed letter name. Gordon calls letter names “the alphabet of music”: knowing them is not the same as audiating, but once you can already read, they explain the notation you understand (Gordon 36–37). That is the order you have learned in: sound first, then syllables, now letters.

Press ▶ to hear an example, or ▶ Sing to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.

What you know → what the book calls it

You say (MLT) The book says (Hutchinson ch. 1)
do, re, mi … (they move with the do signature) letter names A–G (they never move)
“do is on the second line” “do is G”, the letter of that line
the same pattern sung higher or lower the same letters in a different octave register (C4, C5 …)
a note outside the tonality (a chromatic) a note with an accidental (♯ ♭ ♮)
one sound, two spellings enharmonic notes (F♯ = G♭)

1.1–1.2 Pitch and the staff

The book’s first sections cover what you already use: higher and lower sounds, the five-line staff, and the clefs that fix which line is which letter. Read 1.1 · Read 1.2

Syllables move, letters stay. Your syllables are tied to do: move the do signature and every syllable moves with it. Letters are tied to the clef: in treble clef the second line is always G, whatever the signature. So the question changes from “where is do?” to “what letter is do on?”

A note’s name and a note’s job

A letter name is a note’s name: G is G in every key, in every piece. A syllable is the note’s job in the music you’re hearing: home (do), the dominant (so), the leading tone that pulls home (ti). Change the key and the same note gets a new job.

The circle of fifths shows both at once. The outer ring is the letters, and they never move. The inner ring is the syllables. Pick a new key with the menu, or click a letter on the wheel, and watch the syllables turn while the letters stay put. Follow one note, say G: it’s so in C, do in G, re in F, ti in A♭. The note keeps its name and changes its job.

The same works for the book’s other names. Choose scale degrees as the note names (in the Drone or Circle settings), and the inner ring shows 1̂ to 7̂ instead: degree numbers are jobs too.

Here is a tonic pattern, do–mi–so–mi–do, in the treble clef and in the bass clef. Same syllables, same letters, an octave apart:

A way in from what you know. The letters run A B C D E F G and start again. Sing do re mi fa so la ti do in C and say the letters instead: C D E F G A B C. In the key of C, do re mi and C D E line up, which makes C a good place to learn the letters.

Practise: name the note

Treble and bass clef, no accidentals. Open Settings to add ledger lines and accidentals.

1.3 Octave registers

The same letter comes back every eight notes. The book tells them apart with a number: middle C is C4, the C an octave above is C5, and each number runs from C up to the B above it. Read 1.3

You already know this as “the same pattern, higher”. In the two examples above, the treble pattern starts on C4 and the bass pattern on C3.

NoteThe same registers in ABC and LilyPond

Text notations write the register with letter case and marks instead of a number.

Note ABC LilyPond (absolute)
C2 C,, c,
C3 C, c
C4 (middle C) C c'
C5 c c''
C6 c' c'''
  • ABC: a capital letter is the octave from middle C (C4–B4) and a lower-case letter the octave above (C5–B5). Each , takes a note down an octave and each ' takes it up one. The C major scale from middle C is C D E F G A B c.
  • LilyPond: a plain letter is the octave below middle C (C3–B3), and each ' or , moves it an octave, so middle C is c'. The same scale is c' d' e' f' g' a' b' c''.
  • The trap: LilyPond’s plain c is C3 but ABC’s plain C is C4, so the same-looking letter is an octave apart.
  • LilyPond’s \relative mode (common in published files) works differently: each note is placed nearest the note before it, and ' or , only marks a jump of more than a fourth.

1.4–1.5 Accidentals and enharmonic notes

A sharp (♯) raises a note a half step, a flat (♭) lowers it, and a natural (♮) cancels either. In a key signature they apply to the whole piece; written in the music, to the rest of the bar. Read 1.4 · Read 1.5

From what you know. A key signature’s sharps and flats are what put the half steps on mi–fa and ti–do (see Chapter 2). An accidental in the music marks a note outside that pattern, a chromatic. You hear it as a new syllable: in harmonic minor, so is raised to si (Gordon 70), and the music shows it with a sharp or natural.

Enharmonic notes sound the same but are spelled differently: F♯ and G♭, or B and C♭. Which spelling is right depends on the key, just as which syllable is right depends on the tonality. In D major, the note between F and G is F♯, because D major is spelled with one of each letter: D E F♯ G A B C♯.

Where the book and MLT see this differently. Gordon warns against learning letters, accidentals and key signatures before audiating (Gordon 36–37, 65). You haven’t: you’re learning them now, as names for music you can already read.

Bridging: from syllables to letters

  1. Find do and name it. “Do signature of two sharps: do is on D.”
  2. Sing the pattern on syllables, then again on letters: do mi so → D F♯ A.
  3. Every letter in the signature is altered everywhere. In two sharps, every F and every C is sharp, in any octave.
  4. Write in both clefs. Write the pattern in treble, then an octave lower in bass. The letters stay the same; the lines and spaces change.

Check yourself

  1. Treble clef: what letter is the second line? Bass clef: what letter is the fourth line?
  2. Do is on G. Sing do–mi–so. What are the letters?
  3. Which C is middle C, as an octave register?
  4. Give the enharmonic spelling of D♯.
  5. Two sharps are F♯ and C♯. With do on D, which syllable is C♯?
TipAnswers
  1. G (treble), F (bass).
  2. G B D.
  3. C4.
  4. E♭.
  5. Ti.

All the note drills are on Theory Drills. Next: Major Scales and Key Signatures.
